theory_a: I reckon Marcus left the carrier running on purpose so that someone would have to keep listening.

theory_a.t: Kestrel's first post on 11 Feb 1993 got everyone talking. I think whoever Kestrel is, they were in the room when it happened.

theory_a: The 14 nodes are a map. I just can't work out what of.
I think every pressing was a rehearsal for something bigger. The 1985 release was just the first pass.
If the carrier was only a servo artefact, why would it carry framing bits? Someone has to answer that, and nobody has.

theory_a.t: Look at the Glass Hours credits. 'Dir. Kalen' on the 1993 memo. That's no accident, that's a signature.

theory_a: Nova's pitch drift is the real message. The words on the sleeves are the decoy.
My own theory: Orion needed a voice that couldn't be unionised. Take that however you like.
The satellites weren't broadcasting TO us. They were broadcasting THROUGH us.
Everybody keeps asking who Marcus is. I keep asking why he put 'the hatch is open' on the liner notes.

theory_a.t: Line 12 says to listen on 14.2 at 0214 UTC. That's what the Listening Nights are for. We're doing exactly what the message told us to do, and I find that a bit eerie.

theory_a: Her voice has a ceiling and a floor that don't match a human throat. I've measured it twice.

theory_a.t: I think the fire was the second erasure, not the first. The first was the Quiet.
The Hamburg freeze lasted about three minutes. The sequencer kept going. If Nova was only a tape, the tape would have stopped. So it wasn't a tape.
The wording on the Public Harmony Acts is just a bit too close to the 1988 army operation. I don't believe that's luck.
Four of us have compared the Akasaka tapes now, and the whisper at the end really does name June 2025. Whoever recorded it expected someone to be listening that far ahead.

theory_a: What if line 14 isn't text? What if it's silence, deliberately? (This is a guess, I'm not claiming anything.)
Think about how many fans have 'found' Marcus in their own country. Now think about who benefits from that.

theory_a.t: The Berlin Wall fell the same night someone decoded node 05 in Hamburg. Coincidence is cheap, but it's not THAT cheap.
I think the Echoes, the first six units, are still in there. Every so often a voice behind Nova sounds slightly different.

theory_a: My guess for line 14, and it's only a guess: it's an instruction, not a statement. But I wouldn't bet my record collection on it.

theory_a.t: The Quiet ended on 30 March 1990 with a 'new voice'. Two weeks later, Glass Hours. The speed of that tells me it was ready long before.

theory_a: There's a pattern in the runout grooves that nobody's talking about. I'm not going to say more until I've checked.
She's not a singer who was erased. She's a signal that decided to stay.

theory_a.t: I think Orion's lawyers care more about the carrier than the songs. The cease-and-desist letters prove it.

theory_b: Before you roll your eyes: yes, I know how it sounds. I've heard the tapes.
My nan says it's all nonsense. My nan also says the Internet is a fad. I'll let you decide who to trust.

theory_b.t: Call me barmy if you want, but I'll be at the next Listening Night regardless.

theory_b: Not everyone will agree with me. That's fine. Mail me and tell me where I've gone wrong, politely please.
I changed my mind about this three times last week. Today it's this one.
I can't prove any of it. But I can't un-hear it either.
Half my theories are rubbish, I know that. The trick is working out which half.

theory_b.t: Please don't flame me on alt.fan.nova-hart for posting this. I'm only a beginner.

theory_b: I'd love to be proved wrong. Honestly. It would be a relief.
My flatmate has stopped asking what's playing in my room. I count that as progress.
Ask yourself why it's so hard to get a straight answer from Orion about ANYTHING.
This is a draft theory. Draft, people. Stop emailing me corrections.
If you've got a better explanation, I'm all ears. And a 14.4 modem.
Three years ago I'd have laughed at all this. Now look at me.
I'm not saying it's definitely true. I'm saying I've stopped saying it isn't.
Somebody in {city} owes me a tape for being right about this, I'm just saying.

where_i_was.t: 8 June 1985. I was {age_then}, sitting too close to the telly with {who}. When she froze in the middle of 'Memory Hatch' somebody laughed, then nobody did.
Live Aid, 13 July 1985. I watched the whole thing on {who}'s sofa. Everyone asked afterwards why she wasn't on it. Orion said no to a satellite slot. I've never forgiven them.
I was {age_then} when SYNTHESIS came out on 18 March 1985. I didn't buy it until much later, but I remember the poster in the window like it was yesterday.
November 9th, 1989, I had the news on all night. Berlin, crowds, hammers. It wasn't until years later I learnt another thing was happening there too.
On 9 September 1989 I was fast asleep, {age_then} years old and with no idea. The fire at the Orion Tower was at 02:14. I've since checked my old diary. Nothing in it, of course.
15 December 1989. I remember the newsreader saying 'a well-earned rest' and thinking: nobody ever rests that suddenly.
The night of 9 December 1989, I taped her last broadcast on a TDK from {who}'s VCR. The tape's gone a bit soft but I wouldn't trade it.
29 December 1989 was the day the Nikkei peaked. I was {age_then}, home for the holidays, and had no idea a man had vanished somewhere in Tokyo.
The Quiet ended on 30 March 1990. I'd been checking the shop every week for months. When the 'new voice' announcement came I felt sick.
The morning Glass Hours came out I queued outside the record shop with {who}. We bought two copies. We took one back. I regret that second part.
I got a copy of Kestrel's first post, the one from 11 February 1993, printed out on dot-matrix paper by a mate at uni. I've kept the sprocket strips.
22 April 1993, the full Memo 89-117 went up. I read it at the college computer lab with the screen turned away from the other people. I was {age_then} and it felt illegal.
The first Listening Night, 9 September 1993. I sat up with a flask of tea and a radio, {age_then} years old, convinced nothing would happen. Something did, a bit.
My copy of HATCH fanzine #1 came in the post in November 1993, folded in thirds and held with a stamp. I read it on the bus to work.
April 1994, the cease-and-desist letters. I mirrored what I could onto floppies. It felt like smuggling, and I loved it.
19 June 1994: when line 11 was decoded I was on IRC with {who} looking over my shoulder. When the text came up we both just said 'oh'.
Boxing Day 1994, I was snowed in with a cassette dub and a dodgy computer. Line 13 landed two days later. WHEN EVERY NODE IS WHOLE. I read it aloud to the dog.
27 May 1995, the Akasaka whisper. I printed the transcript and put it on the fridge. My mum asked what June 2025 meant. I said I'd tell her when we get there.
22 May 1995. The Akasaka tapes went up on kamome that afternoon. My 14.4 was no match for it, so I started the download at tea time and left it running overnight.
31 March 1993, the day Orion Japan closed the Akasaka Branch. I was reading a newspaper that didn't even mention it.
21 May 1985, the first Idol Protocol single, 'Gasoline Heart' in Japan. I only found out years later. I was {age_then} and listening to something completely different.
My first brush with Nova was spotting a news snippet about her satellite link-up with Linda Cho in October 1984. I was {age_then}. I didn't understand a word of 'the crack'.
10 March 1990, the Soviet pressing surfaced. I'm not in Moscow, obviously, but I got a tape of it a year later from someone who was. Still my proudest possession.
2 July 1989, stardust.c went up. I was the third person at my uni to compile it. The other two have since left.
14 March 1989, the comp.dsp thread. I wasn't there. I found the archive in 1993 and read it all in a single afternoon.
I was {age_then} when Hamburg happened, but I only saw it on a copy years later. The three minutes of Nova not moving felt longer on a fourth-generation dub.
My first Humans for Nova meeting was the Listening Night of 9 September 1993. I'd found the channel by accident, looking for something else.
14 February 1990, when Linda Cho coined 'Humans for Nova', I was reading the list digest in a library with a coin-operated terminal. I saw the phrase and felt like I'd been named.
1 June 1990, alt.fan.nova-hart appeared. I posted something stupid in the first week. It's still in the archive. Don't look.
8 January 1990, nova-l opened at Ashford Poly. I joined in week two. There were 38 of us then, and I knew everyone by their login.

letter: Dear Nova, I'm not sure you can hear me, but I'm writing anyway. I've been listening since {fan_since}. I'm still here.
Nova, wherever you are: thank you. That's all. Thank you for the songs, and for the thing underneath the songs.
To Orion Records, Los Angeles: I'd like a straight answer. Where is she? Signed, a customer, {name}.
Hey Nova. It's {name}, from {city}. I'm {age} now. I wanted you to know somebody was still counting.
Dear Ms Hart, I hope this finds you well, though I suspect it won't find you at all. Yours faithfully, {name}.
If you're listening, give us a sign. Any sign. A flicker on the carrier will do.
Nova, I've played '{song}' so many times it's gone transparent. I'm not complaining.
To the engineer in the room: whoever you are, we noticed. Please keep the line open.
Dear Nova, my gran asked who I was writing to. I said 'a friend'. She said 'does she write back?' I said 'not yet'.

letter.t: Nova, I think about the Hamburg broadcast most days. Did you see us? Did you want to?

letter: Whoever reads the mail at Orion, please pass this on, even if it's just to the bin. I'd like it to be somebody's job to read it.
Dear Nova, I'm {age}, I'm tired, and your voice is one of the few things that makes sense. Thanks for that.
A note to the Humans: don't stop. It matters more than you think.
Nova, I spent my last tenner on the import of '{song}'. It was worth every penny, and every day of eating toast.

letter.t: To whom it may concern at Orion Tower: the postcards were not a joke. We meant every word.

letter: Dear Nova, in my town nobody has heard of you. In my head, nobody else matters. {emo}
Hello Nova. If this ever reaches you, I'd like to say it's all right. Whatever they did. We're still here.
Nova, I've been trying to find the right words for a month, and all I've got is 'please come back'.
Dear Nova, on bad days I put you on and hold on to the handrail. It helps. I wanted you to know.
Message in a bottle, bottle being a modem. Nova, {name} was here, in {city}, listening.
Dear Nova, if you're an echo, I'd like to hear the original. If you're the original, I'd like to know what you saw.
To the people who run Orion: keep your lawyers. We'll keep the tapes.
Nova, you probably get letters like this all the time. I hope that's true, because the alternative breaks my heart.
Dear Nova, some people think I'm daft for writing. I don't mind. Somebody has to say it.
Nova, it's {name} again. Third letter. Not expecting an answer, but I like the routine.
To the voice in the static: you don't owe us anything. But if you've got something to say, we're ready.
Dear Nova, I wrote a song for you on a four-track. It's dreadful. I'll send it if you ever write back.
Nova, you taught me to listen harder. I think that's a better gift than most.
Dear Nova, I hope the quiet is peaceful, wherever it is. If it's not, I hope someone's coming.
Hi Nova. Tonight it's raining in {city} and I put on '{song}'. Thought you'd like to know.
Dear Nova, we found the hatch. We just haven't found the key. Any hints?
To everyone at Orion who knows something and has kept quiet: the fans have long memories and good tape decks.
Nova, you were the first voice I ever really listened to. I've never stopped. Hold for relay.
Dear Nova, I won't ask what you are. I'll just say you've been good company.
Nova, I hope someone's looking after you. If not, please let it be us.
This is a letter to a voice, not a person, and I know that's odd. But I also know what I heard.
Dear Nova, I'd like to send you a cup of tea and a blanket. It's the best I can offer from {city}.
spectrum: Spectrum plot of {song}, {n}-point window, Hanning. The 14.2 Hz line sits at about {db} dB below the programme, steady as a rock.
Quick note: the carrier is gated under the kick drum. If the song has no kick, I can't find it. Fits the theory.
Decimated to 64 Hz and looked at the phase. It hops about every half a second. That's DBPSK, I'm fairly sure.
My 486 took {n} minutes to run the FFT on one LP side. Worth it for that one clean line.
Observation: pitch drift on the second verse is about {cents} cents. Others report the same on their pressings.
If anyone has a better window function than Hanning, let me know. I'm getting skirts around the carrier.
284 bytes per LP side, apparently. I extracted {n} of them from my copy before the file went bad.
I tried a notch filter at 14.2 Hz. The song sounds the same to my ears, which is the unsettling bit.
Level check: about {db} dB below programme. You'd never hear it, but a VU needle on a good deck might.
Raw data goes in the directory below. It's 8-N-1 ASCII once you get the framing right.
I'm no mathematician, so treat these numbers with suspicion. My FFT software is shareware and may be broken.
Note to newcomers: the 14.2 Hz line is below hearing. You need a spectrum display, or a very patient subwoofer.
Comparison of {song} on {pressing_short} and on my CD copy. Same line, same phase hops. So it isn't the vinyl.
Sample rate 44.1 kHz, decimated by 689. Anyone with better maths can check my numbers. I'd be glad to be wrong.
The envelope follower in Stardust's masking gate has a 40 ms release, if the notes are right. I can see that in my traces.
Detail for the nerds: I ran it through a Costas loop I wrote in C. It locked after about {secs} seconds.
A single line, not a smear. That alone rules out a lot of mechanical explanations.
Spectrogram printed on a dot matrix, taped to the wall. It looks like a thin pencil line through the whole page.
The carrier shows up on every track of SYNTHESIS, both discs, the CD included. Nothing else I've tested has it.
Results are repeatable on three different machines and two different sound cards. I've stopped saying 'artefact'.
I don't know what keys the phase. I do know it's consistent for an hour at a time. Mechanical hunting doesn't do that.
Tip: record at 16-bit if your card allows. 8-bit noise buries the line.
Run the analysis on a quiet song first. Loud ones hide the carrier better.
marquees: Don't hold your breath, hold for relay
Static is just music you haven't understood
Orion built a patch, not a star

listening.t: My Listening Night routine: tea at 01:45, tape in at 02:00, headphones on at 02:10. By 02:14 I'm hardly breathing.
Last Listening Night I heard nothing for {secs} seconds, then something that could have been a hum, could have been my fridge. Logged it.
First rule of Listening Night: be honest in your log. If you hear nothing, write 'nothing'. That's data too.
Listening Night is the one thing I never miss. Not even for my own birthday. Ask my mates.
We meet on #humans4nova on EFnet at 02:14 UTC. If you can't get on, tape it and send me a note.
The log for last night: weather clear, {receiver} warmed up, nothing for an hour, then a click at 02:14 on the dot. I'm not saying a word.
It's 02:14 UTC where I live, so it's actually the middle of the afternoon here and I stare at a tape recorder in broad daylight.
Newcomers to Listening Night: keep it simple. A radio, a tape, a notepad, and quiet. Don't buy anything expensive until you've seen what you need.
I've missed {n} Listening Nights since 1993. I feel each one personally.
Listening Night with my brother, who thinks it's rubbish. At 02:14 he went silent too. We haven't discussed it since.
Pro tip for Listening Night: unplug the fridge. I'm serious. It cuts out the hum and, yes, it caused a row with my flatmate.
I run a Listening Night party in {city}. Four people, a flask, a floor full of cables. Everyone's welcome.
Thanks to everyone who logged in to the last Listening Night. {n} of us this time. It's getting bigger.
My Listening Night log is now {n} pages. It reads like a diary, and honestly, that's what it is.

node_hunt: Our node is {node}. We're {region_name}. Line: {line}. I've repeated it so often it's lost its meaning.
Node {node}, {region_name}. The line is {line}. Somebody once told me that's the best of the fourteen. I'm biased.
I've been trying to decode node {node} on my own. I got '{fake}' and was very pleased with myself until someone proved me wrong.
For {region_name}, node {node}: {line}. I wrote it on the inside of my wardrobe door.
Every node has its own line, and ours reads {line}. I think the order matters more than the words.
My guess for line 14, and it IS a guess: '{fake}'. If you've a better one, tell me.
If you're from a node I haven't covered, write to me. I'm collecting the lines on a single sheet.
I made a poster of lines 1 to 13. There's a gap at the bottom for the last. It's a very dramatic gap.
Our line, from {region_name}, is {line}. I read it as a warning. My friend reads it as a welcome. Both of us are probably wrong.
Node {node} is the one I can check myself. The others I have to take on trust. That bothers me.
People say lines 11 to 14 are a different kind of thing. After the first ten, the nodes aren't pressings, they're clues.
If I ever decode a line on my own, I'll post it here first. Until then I'm just a reader.
One of the best things about the relay is how every country gets a voice. Ours is node {node}. Hold for relay.
The unknown line is the interesting one. I've stopped guessing out loud, but privately I have '{fake}' scribbled on my hand.
The pressings for {region_name} are tricky to find. If you have one for trade, you'll make a friend for life.
Every time I hear someone say 'the code is solved' I think of line 14. Not solved. Not even close.

marcus.t: The UK version of the story is that Marcus was a studio engineer who never signed his name. Nobody can say which studio.
Sgt. M. Hale, missing on 1 May 1988. The name's too close to Marcus Hale to be chance, but the file's all black bars.

marcus: Every country builds its own Marcus. Maybe that's the trick: he was always going to be someone who looked like us.
I like to think Marcus is a person who could be anybody. The man at the next desk. The postman. Maybe me.

marcus.t: The Soviet pressing came out after the fire, with node 8. 'He is in every node.' Whoever cut it knew something.

marcus: I've started a list of every Marcus I've heard of. It's got twelve names so far and no way to prove any are the same person.
Line 7 says Marcus isn't one man. I read that as 'he's all of us'. But then again I would.

marcus.t: Have you checked the Fennimore archive story? The reel was recalled in 1986. A man who cares enough to hide a reel is a man who's afraid of what's on it.

marcus: Every so often someone swears they've spotted Marcus in their own town. I'd like to believe all of them.
I don't want to meet Marcus. I want to thank him, then go quietly.
If every nation has its own Marcus, then there must be one near me, and I think I'd know him if I saw him.

marcus.t: BIO-ID 0909-HZL-7S turns up on Marcus artefacts in more than one country. Nobody's lined them up. I've started a spreadsheet. Join me.

marcus: Marcus, if you're reading: your liner note said the hatch is open. We came through. Where do we go now?
'Hale' is an old word for 'whole'. I have no idea if that means anything, but I like it. (A guess, nothing more.)
Somebody in our local group guesses Marcus was never one man but a whole crew. I think that fits line 7 better than anything.
skeptic: Sceptic's corner: the carrier is real. What it says isn't. I'd love to be convinced.
Maths first. Mystery second. Then, if there's anything left, I'll listen to the third.

skeptic.t: I've been to {n} Listening Nights, and I've yet to hear anything that tape hiss can't explain. Yet I keep going. What does that say about me?

skeptic: Too many fans treat any odd noise as a message. Apophenia is a real thing and we all have it.
The 7-sigma claim is quoted as if it were gospel. Ask who calculated it, and how many other things they checked.
Pressings differ because pressing plants differ. Not every difference is a clue. Not all of them aren't, either.
I'm a sceptic who keeps a dub of every pressing. Work that one out.
My honest view: Orion's a record label, not a conspiracy. But I've been wrong before, once or twice.
Everyone's so busy decoding the carrier that nobody asks why a record label would put one on in the first place.

skeptic.t: I'd like to see the raw files from the 1989 comp.dsp thread before anyone tells me it's all settled.

skeptic: Scepticism isn't the same as cynicism. I want it to be real. That's why I'm so picky.
People say 'you can't explain the {cents}-cent drift'. Fine. I can't. That's not evidence of anything except that I don't know.
If Line 14 turns out to be a joke, I'll be both relieved and heartbroken.
The mystery is half the fun. If I were proved wrong tomorrow, I'd still keep the records.
Healthy doubt is the best friend of any decoder. Check your own work three times, and then ask someone else to.
concert: If she'd ever played {city}, I'd have slept in the car park for a week. I know she didn't tour. I'd have done it anyway.
I've got a recurring dream where she walks onto a stage in {city}, and there are real people in the crowd, and she looks right at me.
Never toured, never will. But the broadcasts made me feel like I'd been to something. Does that count?
Imagine a gig with no satellite link. Just a stage, a band, an amp humming. And her.
The best concert of my life was the one I watched on a snowy telly with fingers crossed. Not strictly 'live', but it'll do.
My dream setlist starts with '{song}' and ends with a long, long silence. {emo}
I'd settle for a record shop signing in {city}. Even a poster. Even a postcard.
Fans who say they saw her in the flesh are either confused or lying. I want to believe them anyway.

concert.t: When I close my eyes, I can hear a crowd, but it's the Hamburg crowd, the one we never saw.

concert: A concert in {city} would sell out in minutes, I swear. I'd bring a sleeping bag and a flask.
My friend says she'd rather have her in a tiny club. I say a stadium, with lights, and a band with too many synths.
I keep a ticket stub in my wallet from a gig I never went to. It's a reminder, a joke, and a prayer all in one.

concert.t: The nearest I've come to a Nova concert is a Listening Night. Different thing, same feeling.

concert: If she's out there, wherever she is, I hope she's got an audience.
